test_text.title: Alfred Wegener: science, exploration and the theory of continental drift

article.title: Alfred Wegener: science, exploration and the theory of continental drift
glossary: * Paleoclimatology: The study of past climates

items.sentence_raw: This is a book about the life and scientific work of Alfred Wegener, whose reputation today rests with his theory of continental displacements, better known as 'continental drift'.
Wegener proposed this theory in 1912 and developed it extensively for nearly 20 years.
His book on the subject, "The Origin of Continents and Oceans", went through four editions and was the focus of an international controversy in his lifetime and for some years after his death.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says Wegener's book was *'the focus of an international controversy in his lifetime'* — **'controversy'** means people argued about it, which matches **'widely disputed'**. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Wegener's basic idea was that many mysteries about the Earth's history could be solved if one supposed that the continents moved laterally, rather than supposing that they remained fixed in place.

Wegener showed in great detail how such continental movements were plausible and how they worked, using evidence from a large number of sciences including geology, geophysics, paleontology, and climatology.
items.explain: Q29: The passage says Wegener used evidence from *'a large number of sciences'* — this directly contradicts the question's claim of a **'limited range'**. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Wegener's idea - that the continents move - is at the heart of the theory that guides Earth sciences today: namely plate tectonics.

Plate tectonics is in many respects quite different from Wegener's proposal, in the same way that modern evolutionary theory is very different from the ideas Charles Darwin proposed in the 1850s about biological evolution.
items.explain: Q30: The passage says plate tectonics is *'in many respects quite different from Wegener's proposal'* — this directly contradicts the question's claim that similarities are **'enormous'**. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Yet plate tectonics is a descendant of Alfred Wegener's theory of continental drift, in quite the same way that modern evolutionary theory is a descendant of Darwin's theory of natural selection.
When I started writing about Wegener's life and work, one of the most intriguing things about him for me was that, although he came up with a theory on continental drift, he was not a geologist.
items.explain: Q31: The passage says *'one of the most intriguing things about him for me'* — this is the author's personal view, which matches **'biographer's perspective'**. So the answer is **I**.

items.sentence_raw: He trained as an astronomer and pursued a career in atmospheric physics.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says he *'pursued a career in atmospheric physics'* — this was his main job, which matches **'professional interests'**. So the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: When he proposed the theory of continental displacements in 1912, he was a lecturer in physics and astronomy at the University of Marburg, in southern Germany.
However, he was not an 'unknown'.
items.explain: Q33: The passage says *'he was not an unknown'* and he had *'made a name for himself'* — this means he had some fame, but not huge fame, which matches **'modest fame'**. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: In 1906 he had set a world record (with his brother Kurt) for time aloft in a hot-air balloon: 52 hours.

items.sentence_raw: As important as Wegener's work on continental drift has turned out to be, it was largely a sideline to his interest in atmospheric physics, geophysics, and paleoclimatology*, and thus I have been at great pains to put Wegener's work on continental drift in the larger context of his other scientific work, and in the even larger context of atmospheric sciences in his lifetime.
This is a 'continental drift book' only to the extent that Wegener was interested in that topic and later became famous for it.

My treatment of his other scientific work is no less detailed, though I certainly have devoted more attention to the reception of his ideas on continental displacement, as they were much more controversial than his other work.
Readers interested in the specific detail of Wegener's career will see that he often stopped pursuing a given line of investigation (sometimes for years on end), only to pick it up later.
I have tried to provide guideposts to his rapidly shifting interests by characterizing different phases of his life as careers in different sciences, which is reflected in the titles of the chapters.
Thus, the index should be a sufficient guide for those interested in a particular aspect of Wegener's life but perhaps not all of it.
My own feeling, however, is that the parts do not make as much sense on their own as do all of his activities taken together.
items.explain: Q37: The author says the parts *'do not make as much sense on their own'* and urges readers to experience the whole life — this explains why reading the **whole book** is good. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: In this respect I urge readers to try to experience Wegener's life as he lived it, with all the interruptions, changes of mind, and renewed efforts this entailed.
items.explain: Q37: The author says the parts *'do not make as much sense on their own'* and urges readers to experience the whole life — this explains why reading the **whole book** is good. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Wegener left behind a few published works but, as was standard practice, these reported the results of his work - not the journey he took to reach that point.
Only a few hundred of the many thousands of letters he wrote and received in his lifetime have survived and he didn't keep notebooks or diaries that recorded his life and activities.

He was not active (with a few exceptions) in scientific societies, and did not seek to find influence or advance his ideas through professional contacts and politics, spending most of his time at home in his study reading and writing, or in the field collecting observations.
items.explain: Q38: The passage says Wegener *'did not seek to find influence or advance his ideas'* — this means he was not trying hard to get ahead, which matches **'not a particularly ambitious person'**. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Some famous scientists, such as Newton, Darwin, and Einstein, left mountains of written material behind, hundreds of notebooks and letters numbering in the tens of thousands.
Others, like Michael Faraday, left extensive journals of their thoughts and speculations, parallel to their scientific notebooks.
The more such material a scientist leaves behind, the better chance a biographer has of forming an accurate picture of how a scientist's ideas took shape and evolved.
items.explain: Q39: The passage says more material gives a biographer a *'better chance... of forming an accurate picture'* — this means scientists like Wegener, who left little, are harder to write about. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: I am firmly of the opinion that most of us, Wegener included, are not in any real sense the authors of our own lives.

We plan, think, and act, often with apparent freedom, but most of the time our lives 'happen to us', and we only retrospectively turn this happenstance into a coherent narrative of fulfilled intentions.
items.explain: Q40: The passage says *'most of the time our lives happen to us'* — this means we do not control most things, which matches **'little control over many aspects of their lives'**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: This book, therefore, is a story both of the life and scientific work that Alfred Wegener planned and intended and of the life and scientific work that actually 'happened to him'.
These are, as I think you will soon see, not always the same thing.
